evidence.title: Olorgesailie & Baringo MSA obsidian transport
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar tephra and radiometric dating of Middle Stone Age horizons
evidence.summary: Geochemically sourced volcanic obsidian and red ochre appear 25–160+ km from volcanic outcrops in East African Rift MSA assemblages.
evidence.limits: Direct hand-to-hand exchange cannot be separated from extended group mobility; dots mark excavated findspots rather than quarries.

evidence.title: Southern Levant Cappadocian & Anatolian obsidian hubs
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon stratigraphy and trace-element obsidian characterization
evidence.summary: PPNA el-Hemmeh and Pottery Neolithic Hagoshrim IV show sustained acquisition of central and eastern Anatolian obsidian alongside kin-based exchange partnerships.
evidence.limits: Multiple coastal, Jordan Valley, and desert pathways shifted across Neolithic and Chalcolithic horizons.

evidence.title: Mahal Teglinos & Naqada Horn-to-Nile obsidian link
evidence.dateBasis: Gash Group ceramics, Pharaonic sealings, and obsidian geochemistry
evidence.summary: Eastern Sudan’s Gash Delta hosted Pharaonic trade links and sat astride terrestrial/Nilotic corridors carrying Ethiopian Rift obsidian toward Naqada Upper Egypt.
evidence.limits: Ethiopian quarry provenance is robust, whereas exact intermediate overland stages between the Horn, Kassala, and Upper Egypt remain reconstructed.

evidence.title: Mersa/Wadi Gawasis Pharaonic Red Sea harbor
evidence.dateBasis: Middle Kingdom stelae, cedar ship timbers, and Eritrea/Yemen obsidian sourcing
evidence.summary: Ancient Saww yielded dismantled cedar rigging and Eritrean (Kusrale) and Yemeni (Dhamar) obsidian, while temple baboon isotopes confirm long-range voyages toward Punt.
evidence.limits: Punt encompassed southern Red Sea coastal zones across northeastern Africa and southwestern Arabia rather than one single port.

evidence.title: Kerma metallurgy & Upper Nile trade entrepôt
evidence.dateBasis: Kerma Classique stratigraphy, alloy chemistry, and lead isotope kohl analyses
evidence.summary: Kerma transitioned from arsenical copper to tin bronze and participated in Pharaonic–Nubian exchange of Eastern Desert copper/galena, gold, ivory, and Red Sea shells.
evidence.limits: Local Kushite autonomy and reciprocal Egyptian-Nubian interaction fluctuated across Old and Middle Kingdom frontiers.

evidence.title: Kalba & Dahwa Early Bronze Age Gulf–Oman hubs
evidence.dateBasis: Umm an-Nar monumental tombs, ceramic petrography, and lapis provenance
evidence.summary: Southeastern Arabian ports and Umm an-Nar settlements traded Magan copper and channeled Badakhshan lapis lazuli and Mesopotamian/Indus ceramics across the Gulf.
evidence.limits: Gulf–Oman coastal hubs sit on the Arabian eastern rim linking Middle East Mesopotamia and Africa-Red Sea systems with South Asia.

evidence.title: Kültepe / Kanesh Old Assyrian karum colony
evidence.dateBasis: Old Assyrian cuneiform tablets and Middle Bronze Age stratigraphy
evidence.summary: Over 22,000 cuneiform letters document Assur merchant families operating donkey caravans importing tin and textiles to Anatolian Kanesh in exchange for silver and gold.
evidence.limits: Kültepe archives reflect primarily Assyrian-Anatolian houses; parallel Ebla and Syrian merchant circuits are unevenly preserved.

evidence.title: Mochlos Crete & Eastern Mediterranean tin ingots
evidence.dateBasis: Tin, lead, and trace-element isotope systematics on Late Bronze ingots
evidence.summary: Tin and lead isotope fingerprints match tin ingots from Mochlos (Crete), Uluburun, and Levantine coastal wrecks with Cornish deposits alongside Eurasian supply lines.
evidence.limits: Ore-mixing and maritime transshipment across Sardinian, Iberian, and Anatolian ports complicate single-source attribution.

evidence.title: Faynan & Timna Wadi Arabah copper smelting district
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon-dated slag heaps and archaeometallurgical lead-isotope fingerprints
evidence.summary: Industrial-scale Early Iron Age copper smelting at Faynan (Jordan) and Timna (southern Israel) supplied Negev, Levantine, and Nile Delta metal markets.
evidence.limits: Organization between local Arabah pastoralists and Tel Masos/Levantine intermediaries remains actively debated.

evidence.title: Hama Iron Age grave: verified Baltic amber in Syria
evidence.dateBasis: FTIR spectroscopy on Iron Age cremation-cemetery beads at Hama
evidence.summary: Spectroscopic analysis verifies true Baltic succinite amber beads in Iron Age western Syria, confirming down-the-line trade linking Northern Europe and the Levant.
evidence.limits: Chemically confirms Baltic origin, while intermediate overland versus maritime Adriatic–Aegean stages remain schematic.

evidence.title: Garama & Fewet Garamantian Saharan trade oases
evidence.dateBasis: Fazzan urban excavations, Roman amphorae, glass, and carnelian/amazonite sourcing
evidence.summary: Foggara-irrigated Fezzan cities channeled Roman glass, wine amphorae, carnelian, and green amazonite stone beads along pre-Islamic trans-Saharan networks.
evidence.limits: Southern Sahelian termini are represented archaeologically by imported glass beads and Sahelian/Saharan stone circulation rather than written ledgers.

evidence.title: Meroë, Dangeil & Faras Kushite Nile trade corridor
evidence.dateBasis: Crucible metallurgy, natron glass chemistry, and garnet bead sourcing
evidence.summary: Kushite cities linked Central African/Nubian iron and gold with Eastern Mediterranean tin bronze alloys, Mediterranean natron glass, and South Asian garnets.
evidence.limits: Material imports were selectively integrated into Meroitic ritual and elite identity rather than simple passive emulation.

evidence.title: Petra & Palmyra desert caravan entrepôts
evidence.dateBasis: Negev caravanserai middens, Palmyrene inscriptions, and remote-sensing trackways
evidence.summary: Nabataean Negev caravanserais provisioned incense routes from Petra to Gaza while Palmyra rose as a major caravan metropolis linking Syria to the Euphrates and Persian Gulf.
evidence.limits: Anchor placed at Palmyra; Nabataean Negev stations and Thāj in eastern Arabia are represented along the accompanying corridor route.

evidence.title: Berenike & Myos Hormos Red Sea monsoon ports
evidence.dateBasis: Port stratigraphy, coin assemblages, Eastern Desert praesidia, and Periplus account
evidence.summary: Connected to the Nile at Coptos across fortified Eastern Desert camel tracks, Berenike and Myos Hormos linked Alexandria and Rome with East Africa, Arabia, and India.
evidence.limits: Port activity continued well past 100 CE into Late Antiquity; shown up to the 100 CE focus threshold.

waves.title: East African Rift MSA Obsidian Transport (Olorgesailie–Baringo)
waves.summary: Geochemically provenanced volcanic obsidian and red ochre moved 25–160+ km along East African Rift Middle Stone Age exchange/social networks.
waves.limits: Schematic Rift Valley vector; represents repeated quarry-to-site conveyance rather than formalized caravan trade.

waves.title: Anatolian–Levantine–Central European Neolithic Obsidian Network
waves.summary: Cappadocian (Göllü Dağ) and eastern Anatolian (Nemrut Dağ) obsidian circulated down to the Southern Levant (el-Hemmeh, Hagoshrim) and northwestward ~2,200 km into Neolithic Poland.
waves.limits: Schematic network combining early PPNA Levantine pathways and later Chalcolithic/Neolithic European down-the-line conveyance.

waves.title: Horn of Africa–Eastern Sudan–Upper Egypt Obsidian Corridor
waves.summary: Geochemical tracing assigns Naqada-period Upper Egyptian obsidian to Ethiopian sources, channeled via terrestrial/Nilotic links through Eastern Sudan (Mahal Teglinos).
waves.limits: Intermediate waypoints across Sudan and Eritrea remain sparse; line connects quarry zone, Kassala hub, and Naqada.

waves.title: Badakhshan Lapis Lazuli Corridor: Afghanistan to Mesopotamia, Oman & Egypt
waves.summary: Raw lapis lazuli quarried in Badakhshan moved through Shahr-i Sokhta to Gulf Oman (Dahwa), Ur in Mesopotamia, Ebla in Syria, and royal workshops in Bronze Age Egypt.
waves.limits: Schematic multi-branch arc merging Iranian plateau caravan and Persian Gulf maritime branches.

waves.title: Mesopotamia–Dilmun–Magan–Meluhha Gulf & Arabian Desert Network
waves.summary: Maritime trade linked Ur via Dilmun (Bahrain) and Magan copper ports (Kalba, Oman) to the Indus (Meluhha), paired with a c. 2000 BCE caravan corridor from Dilmun to Wādī al-Fāw.
waves.limits: Combines maritime Gulf sailings and overland Dilmun–Arabian desert caravan finds in one schematic corridor.

waves.title: Egypt–Nubia–Kerma Nile & Eastern Desert Supply Chain
waves.summary: Bronze Age supply chains carried Eastern Desert galena/copper, Egyptian tin bronzes, Nubian gold, and garnets along the Nile Cataracts between Egypt and Kerma.
waves.limits: Control alternated between peaceful Kushite exchange, Kerma hegemony, and New Kingdom imperial fortresses.

waves.title: Pharaonic Red Sea Expeditions to the Land of Punt
waves.summary: Cross-desert tracks from Coptos launched fleets from Mersa/Wadi Gawasis down the Red Sea to Eritrean and Yemeni shores, yielding obsidian, incense, and baboons isotopically matched to the Horn.
waves.limits: Schematic coastal voyage line; seasonal Egyptian expeditions sailed intermittently during Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms.

waves.title: Old Assyrian Assur–Kanesh Caravan & Ebla–Levant Circuit
waves.summary: Textually documented Old Assyrian donkey caravans hauled tin and woolen textiles across northern Mesopotamia to Kanesh in Anatolia, interlocking with Ebla’s Levantine circuit.
waves.limits: Tracks represent main Upper Euphrates and Taurus caravan passes inferred from Kanesh letters and site gravity modeling.

waves.title: Baltic–Adriatic–Aegean–Levant Amber Road
waves.summary: Spectroscopically verified Baltic amber moved south across Central Europe and the Adriatic in exchange for Mediterranean metals and prestige wares, reaching Bronze Age Mycenae and Iron Age Hama in Syria.
waves.limits: Multi-millennium schematic corridor; Bronze/Iron Age exchanges were relay-based, whereas the imperial Roman Amber Road formalized Carnuntum–Aquileia stages.

waves.title: Atlantic–Sardinia–Eastern Mediterranean Tin & Metal Network
waves.summary: Tin and lead isotopes connect Late Bronze Age ingots from Crete (Mochlos), Cyprus, and Levantine wrecks to Cornish ore via Atlantic seaways and Nuragic Sardinian hubs.
waves.limits: Schematic coastal synthesis; Central Asian and Iberian tin also contributed across changing Bronze Age markets.

waves.title: Wadi Arabah (Faynan & Timna)–Negev–Egypt Iron Age Copper Network
waves.summary: High-output Early Iron Age copper smelting at Faynan and Timna fed distribution centers like Tel Masos in the Negev and Egypt’s eastern Delta.
waves.limits: Schematic regional corridor linking mining valleys to Levantine and Egyptian consumers.

waves.title: Kushite & Meroitic Nile–Red Sea–Mediterranean Exchange Corridor
waves.summary: From Napata through Meroë and Dangeil, Kushite workshops imported Mediterranean copper alloys and natron glass alongside South Asian garnets, exporting African ivory, gold, and iron.
waves.limits: Follows generalized Nile corridor; Red Sea caravan outlets via Eastern Sudan and Aksum operated in parallel.

waves.title: Garamantian Trans-Saharan Oasis Trade Network (Fezzan–Mediterranean–Sahel)
waves.summary: The Garamantes of Fezzan linked Mediterranean Tripolitania (Lepcis Magna) via oasis hubs at Garama and Fewet with Central Saharan and Sahelian communities, trading Roman glass, ceramics, carnelian, and amazonite.
waves.limits: Southern extensions beyond Fazzan represent multi-stage oasis relay networks rather than uniform imperial caravans.

waves.title: Early West African Niger River & Sahel Exchange Network
waves.summary: Urbanizing riverine centers in the Inland Niger Delta (Jenné-Jeno) mobilized iron, copper, fish, and ceramics across the Middle Niger bend, later connecting with North African/Near Eastern glass beads.
waves.limits: Early Iron Age long-distance bead imports increase dramatically after 100 CE; line depicts formative pre-100 CE Niger–Sahel river/overland exchange.

waves.title: Nabataean Negev & Palmyrene Syrian Desert Caravan Corridors
waves.summary: Nabataean caravans provisioned across Negev caravanserais from Petra to Gaza, while Hellenistic Thāj and Roman Palmyra linked Syria across the Euphrates to the Persian Gulf.
waves.limits: Unites distinct Nabataean-Red Sea/Negev and Palmyrene-Euphrates caravan organizations on a schematic regional path.

waves.title: Ptolemaic–Early Roman Red Sea & Eastern Desert Corridor (Alexandria–Berenike–Adulis)
waves.summary: Fortified Eastern Desert camel stations linked the Nile at Coptos to Myos Hormos and Berenike, powering Ptolemaic and early Roman Erythraean Sea monsoon fleets toward Aksum/Adulis, Arabia, and India.
waves.limits: Schematic trunk route; continues toward South Asia on the Indian Ocean monsoon corridors.
